vignette:
Margaret is a 79-year-old widow of European American background who has spent most of her adult life working as a tailor, first from a small alterations shop and now from a sewing room she keeps in the front of her house. She came to treatment late in life, after many years of managing alone, and spoke about her military trauma in a way that made clear both how near it still feels and how impossible it has been for her to set it down in words. When she tries to describe what happened, she stops and circles back, losing the order of events. She knows there was blood, knows there were moments of shouting and movement and then a stunned aftermath, but she cannot put the memory into a clean sequence. She becomes visibly tense when she approaches it and then angry, not in a general way but with a sudden, scorching force that seems to seize her as the memory comes close. She says she cannot seem to say it properly, that the worst part lives in images and bodily sensations rather than language.

The event occurred during her military service, and although she has avoided speaking about details for decades, the fragments she does report have remained sharply potent. Blood is the cue she mentions immediately. Even now, the sight of it can pull her out of the present. A nicked finger in her sewing room, a customer joking about “bleeding hems,” a television scene she did not expect to see—these moments strike her with unwanted thoughts she cannot wave off. What comes to her is not a complete story but a rush of vivid, disjointed impressions that make her feel as if she is back in contact with something unfinished and intolerable. Certain conversation topics are almost as difficult. If neighbors begin talking about the military, wartime injuries, or even news stories involving troops, Margaret’s face closes off. She has learned to leave the room, change the subject abruptly, or busy herself with thread and fabric rather than remain exposed to where her mind might go.

In the years after the trauma, she noticed a change she still describes mournfully: she used to think of herself as a happy person, sociable and easy to please, and now she experiences herself as permanently altered. She says she is always miserable, and when she tries to explain that, she does not mean merely sad. She means a kind of deadness, an inner flatness that leaves her feeling emotionally absent from her own life. She has come to believe that nothing good can happen to her anymore. When pleasant moments appear, they do not register as comfort. They feel dangerous, almost like a setup. Because of that, she has gradually built a life organized around not letting herself feel too much hope or warmth. If her granddaughter suggests a family dinner, or an old friend invites her to church tea or a birthday lunch, Margaret often declines. She tells herself it is easier not to go than to risk the jolt of feeling briefly happy and then having that feeling turn unsafe in her body. Over time she has also stopped seeing friends with any regularity. The result is that her world has narrowed to work, errands, and long quiet evenings in the house she once shared with her husband.

Her work as a tailor shows this pattern clearly. Sewing is familiar and structured, and she still takes pride in precise work, but even there the trauma intrudes. A client discussing a son in the service, a finger pricked by a needle, a stain on a garment that resembles blood can suddenly fill her mind with unwanted thoughts. On those days she becomes withdrawn and curt, sometimes closing the shop room early and leaving hems unfinished until the next day. She does not explain this to customers; she simply says she is tired. Friends have learned not to press her, and many have stopped asking.

What finally brought Margaret to seek help was not a single crisis but the recognition, after years of widowhood and increasing isolation, that she was living as though every good thing had to be kept at arm’s length. She recently turned down a visit with relatives she genuinely wanted to see and then sat alone in her sewing room, feeling empty and furious with herself. That moment frightened her. She could see how little of life she was permitting herself. At the same time, she remains afraid of what might happen if she lets the memories come closer or allows herself to feel happiness again. What she hopes for, cautiously, is not to become someone new, but to feel less dead inside and to be able to stay present when ordinary life brushes against the past.
